query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In a high-entropy alloy (HEA) subject to tribo-corrosion, the overall degradation is controlled by a stress‐assisted cyclic breakdown and reformation of a naturally forming protective oxide film. Specifically, mechanical wear intermittently removes the passivating oxide layer, exposing fresh reactive metal that rapidly re-oxidizes due to the presence of oxidation-promoting alloying elements (e.g., Cr, Al). The balance between the rate of oxide removal by wear and oxide reformation governs the coupled corrosion and wear response.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-fabricated HEA composed of elements that promote rapid oxide formation (such as Cr and/or Al) and exhibiting an intact, self-healing passive oxide layer.
generation.intervention: Expose the HEA to simultaneous sliding wear and a corrosive medium (for example, a NaCl aqueous solution) under controlled load and environmental conditions.
generation.conditions: Compare tribo-corrosion behavior (combined mechanical wear and corrosion) to isolated corrosion (no wear) and isolated wear (in inert environment) tests at similar temperatures and mechanical stresses to simulate service conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The integrity and kinetics of the protective oxide film that forms on the surface of the HEA.
generation.mechanism: During tribological contact, mechanical wear disrupts the surface oxide, exposing virgin metal. In the corrosive environment, reactive alloying elements rapidly oxidize to restore the protective film. If wear removes the oxide faster than it can be regenerated, localized corrosion accelerates, enhancing total degradation. Conversely, if oxide regeneration is rapid, a quasi-steady-state condition is achieved that limits both excessive wear and corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a static corrosion baseline, the HEA under tribo-corrosion conditions will exhibit an increased overall degradation rate, with synergistic interactions between wear and corrosion. However, if the oxide can rapidly reform, the wear component may be partially mitigated by a lubricious oxide film, resulting in a complex non‐additive response compared to separate tests.
generation.baseline: The same HEA subjected only to exposure in the corrosive medium without applied mechanical wear, allowing full development of a continuous passive oxide layer.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for HEAs enriched in elements that enable fast oxide regeneration. It may fail or be markedly different in alloys with limited reactive element content or under conditions (e.g., very low oxygen availability or extremely high wear rates) where oxide reformation kinetics are suppressed.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative balance between oxide removal and reformation rates, and thus the exact contributions of wear versus corrosion to the overall degradation, remain uncertain and are likely to be highly dependent on both the detailed alloy composition and test parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one using the target HEA with reactive elements (e.g., Cr/Al) and another compositionally similar alloy lacking these key elements. Subject both sets to identical tribo-corrosion tests under controlled sliding wear in a corrosive NaCl solution. Utilize in-situ surface analytical techniques (e.g., X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy or SEM with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy) to monitor oxide film thickness and continuity over time, and measure overall degradation (weight loss), wear rate, and electrochemical behavior.
measurements: Surface oxide layer thickness and composition (via XPS/SEM-EDX)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the reactive-element-containing HEA does not show evidence of cyclic oxide breakdown and reformation (i.e., similar oxide layer characteristics throughout the test) and its tribo-corrosion degradation rate is statistically indistinguishable from that of the non-reactive alloy, the hypothesis that oxide film dynamics mediate the coupled tribo-corrosion response is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. Abstract Dual-phase high entropy alloys have recently attracted widespread attention as advanced structural materials due to their unique microstructure, excellent mechanical properties, and corrosion resistance. However, their molten salt corrosion behavior has not been reported, which is critical in evaluating their application merit in the areas of concentrating solar power and nuclear energy. Here, the molten salt corrosion behavior of AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was evaluated in molten NaCl-KCl-MgCl 2 salt at 450 °C and 650 °C in comparison to conventional duplex stainless steel 2205 (DS2205). The EHEA showed a significantly lower corrosion rate of ~1 mm/year at 450 °C compared to ~8 mm/year for DS2205. Similarly, EHEA showed a lower corrosion rate of ~9 mm/year at 650 °C compared to ~20 mm/year for DS2205. There was selective dissolution of the body-centered cubic phase in both the alloys, B2 in AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 and α-Ferrite in DS2205. This was attributed to micro-galvanic coupling between the two phases in each alloy that was measured in terms of Volta potential difference using a scanning kelvin probe.
